analysis.one_liner: Requires for-profit and private-equity-owned health care companies to disclose finances and operations and lets HHS block risky takeovers.
analysis.headline: The bill had only 2 cosponsors and sat with four House committees without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Health Over Wealth Act would force for-profit corporations that own hospitals, nursing homes, physician practices, and other health care providers to publicly report their debt, fees, executive pay, staffing levels, and political spending. It would require private equity funds to get a federal license before buying health care companies, let the Health Department block purchases while a task force studies the industry, and require hospitals to give 90 days' notice and a mitigation plan before closing services. It would also strip tax breaks from health care real estate investment trusts and push pension debts to the front of the line in health care bankruptcies.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients in communities served by private-equity-owned or for-profit health facilities would gain transparency and protections against sudden closures, understaffing, and asset-stripping. Health care workers would gain public reporting of wage cuts, vacancy rates, and labor law complaints, and their pension claims would take priority in bankruptcy. Rural communities facing hospital closures would get 90 days' notice, a public comment process, and a mandatory mitigation plan before services disappear. The fees charged for private equity licenses would fund community health centers, the National Health Service Corps, and safety-net hospitals.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every for-profit firm that owns health care providers — and any private equity fund controlling one — to report debt levels, fees charged to the health care business, dividends extracted, executive salaries, staffing ratios, wage reductions, facility closures, and labor law complaints, with the data posted publicly and audited by the Health Department.

Requires private equity firms to obtain a federal license to invest in health care, which the Secretary can deny or revoke for price gouging, understaffing, or access barriers; a revoked firm must divest, and license fees would fund the National Health Service Corps, community health centers, and safety-net hospitals.

Lets the Secretary set up escrow requirements, minimum capital investments, and a possible moratorium on private equity purchases of health care companies until a task force studies whether abuses like understaffing and access barriers are occurring in specific sectors.

Requires hospitals to notify the Secretary at least 90 days before closing or cutting services, bar cutting essential services during the notice period, submit a public mitigation plan, and face a public comment process — with Medicare enrollment ineligibility as the penalty for violations.

Moves pension withdrawal liability to the front of the bankruptcy claims line for health care businesses and requires courts to weigh regional access to care and staff retention when approving health care bankruptcy plans, so workers and retirees are not left behind when a private-equity-owned provider collapses.

Ends the tax benefit for health care real estate investment trusts by excluding rents from health care property from REIT-qualifying income, and prohibits sale-leaseback deals that would weaken a health care entity's finances or put public health at risk.

Requires covered firms and private equity funds to disclose their political spending, including lobbying and contributions related to health care and to members of congressional committees with health care oversight.

analysis.who_pays: Private equity funds, health care real estate investment trusts, and for-profit owners of hospitals, nursing homes, physician practices, and other providers would bear the costs: extensive new reporting, license fees, possible escrow and capital investment requirements, civil penalties, and the loss of REIT tax treatment on health care rents. Patients might see some investment capital pull back from health care acquisitions. The Health Department would take on significant new regulatory and audit work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and for-profit health care owners

drawbacks.text: The reporting and licensing regime is broad — covering debt ratios, vendor lists, staffing, and political spending across every for-profit owner of any Medicare-enrolled provider — and the Secretary's discretion to deny licenses, impose escrow requirements, and block acquisitions could discourage investment in struggling hospitals and nursing homes that owners might otherwise sell or recapitalize.

Requiring a 90-day notice period and prohibiting the discontinuation of essential services during that window could delay closures of money-losing hospitals, and the Secretary can keep a hospital out of Medicare for up to three years for violating the rules, costs that could fall on the facilities' remaining patients and staff.

Putting pension withdrawal liability first in bankruptcy would push other creditors down the priority ladder, which creditors may price into future lending to health care businesses as higher borrowing costs.

Compliance costs for hundreds of pages of financial and operational disclosure would fall on covered firms, and the bill directs the Secretary to reduce duplication only 'to the maximum extent practicable' rather than capping the burden.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core value is information and leverage: patients, workers, and regulators currently have little visibility into how private equity-owned providers are financed, staffed, and stripped, and this bill would put that data on the public record while giving the government real tools to stop harmful takeovers and closures. The honest tradeoffs are real but manageable — broad regulatory discretion could chill some investment in health care, and the reporting burden is heavy — but they are the predictable cost of any serious oversight regime, and the bill includes explicit instructions to avoid duplicative reporting.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2026 with two cosponsors and sent to four House committees, none of which has taken it up, so it has not come anywhere near a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Pramila Jayapal introduced the Health Over Wealth Act in the House on July 23, 2026, joined by Representatives Deluzio and Clarke of New York as cosponsors.

The Speaker referred it to four committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, Ways and Means, and Judiciary — because its provisions span health, tax, securities, and bankruptcy law, which means any consideration requires one committee to take the lead.
No committee has held a hearing or marked up the bill, and the House has not voted on it; the Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill is still technically alive but has not moved.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened beyond introduction, the current rules for private equity funds, health care REITs, and for-profit health care owners remain unchanged — they are better off than they would be under the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and health care REITs, for now

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and is its lead sponsor.

for.name: Reps. Chris Deluzio and Yvette Clarke
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only two cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors are House Democrats, but with no committee action or floor vote there is no record of where most members stand.

industries.industry: Private equity and venture capital funds
industries.note: The bill would require a federal license to buy health care companies, allow a moratorium on new health care purchases, mandate escrow accounts and minimum capital investments, and force public disclosure of fees, debt loads, dividends, and political spending. Funds that lose their license would have to divest from health care entirely.

industries.industry: Health care real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The bill excludes rents from health care property from REIT-qualifying income, removing the tax advantage, and prohibits sale-leaseback deals that would weaken a hospital or nursing home's finances. These sale-leasebacks are a common way private equity extracts cash from health facilities.

industries.industry: For-profit hospital, nursing home, and physician practice owners
industries.note: These firms would have to report finances, staffing, closures, wage cuts, and labor violations publicly, face $10,000-per-violation penalties, and give 90 days' notice with a mitigation plan before closing services. Hospital closures and service cuts are a leading access problem in rural and underserved areas.

Pension withdrawal liability would move to the front of the bankruptcy claims line, and covered firms would have to report wage reductions, vacancy rates, and labor law complaints publicly, with union representatives seated on the bill's task force.

industries.industry: Registered investment companies and asset managers
industries.note: The SEC would get new rulemaking authority to forbid registered funds from stripping assets from health care entities or undermining access to care, adding compliance duties but aimed at protecting the health facilities the funds invest in.

analysis.trajectory: With only two cosponsors, four competing committees, and no hearing scheduled, the bill is very unlikely to advance before the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027; most health policy bills referred to multiple committees late in a session never reach the floor.
